# jochwacht-sbom 0.17.0 — the former name is no longer read either

Up to 0.16.0 this tool still *recognised* the name it was released under
before 0.12.0. It no longer does. The consequence is deliberate, and it is
loud rather than silent.

## Breaking: a bill written by a version before 0.12.0 counts as foreign

`write_cyclonedx` refuses to overwrite a bill of materials it did not
recognise as its own. The set of names it accepts as "ours" now holds only
the current one, so a file produced by a release before 0.12.0 is treated as
somebody else's document — which is exactly what the safeguard is for.

You get an error naming the file and the way out (`--sbom PATH` to write
beside it), not a silent overwrite. If you hold such a file, point the tool
at a new path and keep the old one.

This follows a decision of 29 October 2026 that no installed base carries the
former namespace. If yours does, 0.16.0 remains on PyPI.

## The warning about an unread declaration file stays — it now checks the form

A declaration file (`*-deps.yaml`) carries supplier and license details that
exist nowhere else in a project: when one is present but not read, the bill
comes out quietly thinner. That warning stays. What changed is what it looks
for.

Before, it compared against a list of former spellings. Now it asks a
question about the **form**: is there a `*-deps.yaml` here that is not the one
we read? That still catches the old name, and it additionally catches what the
list never could — a typo such as `jochwach-deps.yaml`, which used to pass
unnoticed. Held by tests.

A name that differs only in case follows the file system, deliberately: on
Linux `Jochwacht-deps.yaml` is a different file, is not read, and is reported;
on Windows and macOS it is the *same* file, so it **is** read, nothing is lost,
and a warning would be false. The test asks the file system rather than
guessing the platform. The Windows matrix of our CI is what found that, after
the first version of the test asserted the Linux answer as the only one.

**The limit, documented as its own test:** for the project configuration
(`*.yaml`) and for exclusion lists (`.*ignore`) there is no form that does
not produce mass false positives — `.gitignore` would be one of them. Those
two cases stay silent. That is defensible because the loss measured on
5 October 2026 concerned the *declaration* file, which carries statements
found nowhere else, whereas a configuration file that is not read only means
defaults were used.

## The name guard reads the whole tree, itself included

The test that forbids the former name no longer spells it out; it composes it
from parts. So it needs no exemption for itself and reads every file,
including its own: **the allowlist is empty** — it held five entries before.

Two counter-proofs were run and both went red as required: the old name
planted in `README.md` (found as `README.md:248`) and a file carrying it in
its path. Both restored from a copy, not from `git`.

Measured on this tree: 222 tests green, `ruff check src tests` without a
finding.
